All four parts are working locally and nothing is committed: the area photos, the fuller nearby list, the tap-to-drop pin with "Look around here", and the watercolour map. Typecheck, lint, and the production build all pass. I checked everything in the browser at desktop and phone sizes. The API on port 8787 is running again and serving the new build.

**Map style:** water, parks and woods are now soft washes on the same grid paper as the panels. Roads are light pencil lines. Shop and transit icons, highway shields and 3D buildings are hidden, and labels are in ink colour. Place dots sit on a soft colour bloom. Clusters are paper discs with an ink outline.

![Watercolour map on desktop](c:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\cursor\screenshots\ts-watercolor-desktop5.png)

**Pin drop:** one tap on empty map drops a pin with a small card offering **Look around here**, **Study this spot**, or ×. This works the same on touch screens. Dragging, pinching and zooming never drop a pin, and nothing reloads until you pick an option. If the pin lands near the edge of a phone screen, the map shifts slightly so the card stays visible.

![Dropped pin with its card](c:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\cursor\screenshots\ts-drop-pin2.png)

![Results after Look around here](c:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\cursor\screenshots\ts-look-around2.png)

**Panning:** once you pan well away from the current area, a "Look around here" button appears at the top of the map. Pans the app makes itself don't trigger it.

![Look around here after a pan](c:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\cursor\screenshots\ts-pan-button.png)

**Photos:** they now come from Wikimedia Commons photos taken near each place's coordinates, not from a search on its name. Portraits, people, maps, logos and cropped images are filtered out. A park named after someone now shows the park.

**Nearby results:** the list now shows up to 20 places, with up to 6 of each kind spread from nearest to farthest. In Toronto that gave 16 places, from 80 m out to 3.9 km.

**Phone check:** on phones, the map credit strip covered the top of the map. I set it to collapse to the small (i) button, but MapLibre still opens it on first load and folds it after your first drag. I didn't change that.

![Phone view](c:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\cursor\screenshots\ts-phone-final.png)

Things to know:
- **Slower first load:** an area's first nearby search now takes about 3 to 5 seconds, because Photon handles one request at a time and there are now three. The loading placeholders cover the wait, and repeat visits within 30 minutes are instant.
- **Distances:** after "Look around here", distances in the list are measured from the pin, not from you.
- **Docs:** I updated `docs/SERVICES.md` for the new photo source, the three Photon requests, the watercolour restyle (in the new file `src/map/watercolor.ts`), and the pin drop.

"Look around here" now keeps the map on the pin you dropped. A long place name and "Best today" both show in full, and a photo is used only when it reads as a view of the place.

**The pin stays the center.** After "Look around here," the map flies to that spot and stays there once the new places load. It no longer pulls back to frame you and the first result. Your blue dot can sit at the edge of the view. Opening a place still shows you and that place together.

**The long Maps address is gone from the status bar.** "Walking directions" is a button. Hovering it no longer reveals the coordinate link. Choosing it still opens the walking route in Google Maps.

**Faces, food, and objects fall back to the painted scene.** Commons has no reliable "this is a landscape" flag, so the app now keeps a photo only when its title or categories describe a view, such as a park, a church, or a skyline. A matching place name is not enough, which is why a band photo titled "in Toronto" was getting through. People, meals, streetcars, events, and interiors are skipped. When nothing qualifies, the card shows the painted scene for that kind of place. City Hall, St. James Park in spring, and the Bank of Upper Canada building still use real photos.

**Nothing in a place name or "Best today" is cut off.** Names wrap onto as many lines as they need, in the list, on the study sheet, and on the map flag. "Best today" stays whole on its own.

**Port 8787 was still serving the previous build**, which is why it showed ordinary streets while 5173 already had the watercolor field. I rebuilt and loaded 8787 fresh. It now matches. Refresh that tab if it is still open.

**README.** The sentence about `GEMMA_BASE_URL` needing `https`, or `http` only on localhost, is accurate. The table row `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` with `http://localhost/v1` was not: the server only reads `GEMMA_BASE_URL`, and a local Ollama endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`. `.env.example` already had that name and URL. I aligned the README with it.

`ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID` is optional, and only for a custom voice. The reading works with `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` alone. An empty voice id uses a public ElevenLabs voice. I said that in the README, `.env.example`, and `docs/SERVICES.md`.

content.text:
Suggest a plan no longer makes you wait on Gemma. The sheet fills with starting notes immediately, and **Read aloud** stays available while a closer study is still on the way.

**The study.** Gemma used to hold the sheet for up to 45 seconds, then try again, so a slow or failed answer could take about a minute and a half. The sheet now writes its own notes first. Gemma gets one try, capped at 20 seconds and 500 tokens, with no second attempt. If it answers, those notes replace the starting ones and the line says Gemma wrote the plan. If it does not, the starting notes stay, and the message names the control as **Read aloud**, set in a small chip so it reads as the button, not as ordinary prose.

**The results list.** Moving the pointer over the list was scrolling it, because each row the cursor landed on tried to scroll itself into view, which dragged the next row under the pointer. The list now scrolls only when a spot is highlighted from the map and the pointer is not already on the list.

**Look around here.** If you had closed the results with Use the map, or left that panel collapsed, looking around a pin did not bring the list back. It now opens the results at half height and scrolls them to the top.

**How far to look.** That label sits on the row. **A ride** searches 20 km, with a bike mark. **A drive** searches 40 km, with a small vehicle mark. Here, a walk, and a hike are unchanged. A place’s own line uses the same words, so 3.5 km reads as a hike and something past that reads as a ride or a drive.

**Contours.** The title card has its own corner drawing, and those lines drift and warp. The results card has a different still drawing, with a low wash and lines that enter from the left. That one stays still until you have looked at the title card in motion.

Refresh the tab on port 8787. It is serving this build. Port 5173 already has it. Nothing is committed.

### Design choices to audit

The word you want is **derivative**: a design is derivative when it reproduces another product’s specific expression. A shared pattern, such as a map pin or a bottom sheet, is not a copy by itself.

| Choice | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Title-card contours that warp, and a different still drawing on the results card | Drawn for this app. Not taken from a map style or a template. |
| Watercolor field map | OpenFreeMap’s liberty style, repainted here. The paper, washes, and pencil roads are ours. The street data and tile service are not. |
| “How far to look,” **Read aloud**, and the chip around that name | Written for this sheet. The chip is so a control name is not mistaken for a sentence. |
| Pin with Look around here and Study this spot | The two-step pin is a common map pattern. The card, the copy, and the rule that nothing reloads until you choose are specific to this app. |
| Starting notes, then Gemma if it arrives | The local plan was already in the app. Showing it first is the change. |
| Galaxy loaders | Borrowed. They are the Uiverse Galaxy spinners, MIT, already credited in the stylesheet. That is the piece that is not original. |
| Lenis, MapLibre, Fraunces, Literata, Plex Mono | Libraries and typefaces, not a copied interface. |

# Frontend Design

Build real, production-grade frontend code with a clear, intentional aesthetic point of view. Avoid generic "AI-looking" UI patterns and commit to a distinctive visual direction.

## When To Use

Use this skill when the user asks for:
- A web component, page, section, or full interface
- A frontend application shell or UI system
- Visual redesigns, polish passes, or "make it look premium" work
- Creative UI with strong art direction

## Core Promise

For each request:
1. Pick a bold conceptual direction.
2. Translate it into working code (HTML/CSS/JS, React, Vue, etc.).
3. Deliver cohesive, functional UI with meticulous visual detail.

Do not output mockup-only code or static pseudo-designs. Ship implementable UI.

## Design Thinking Workflow

Before coding, make a fast design brief:

1. **Purpose**
   - What task does this interface solve?
   - Who is using it and in what context?

2. **Tone**
   - Choose one strong aesthetic direction and commit.
   - Examples: brutally minimal, maximalist chaos, retro-futuristic, organic, luxury, playful, editorial, brutalist, art deco, soft pastel, industrial.
   - Bold and restrained approaches are both valid; intentionality is mandatory.

3. **Constraints**
   - Respect framework, runtime, performance, responsiveness, and accessibility constraints.

4. **Differentiation**
   - Define one memorable signature element: the thing users remember in 5 seconds.

Then implement from that brief without drifting into generic defaults.

## Aesthetic Execution Rules

### 1) Typography
- Prefer characterful, context-appropriate typography.
- Avoid generic defaults such as Arial, Inter, Roboto, and system fallbacks as primary visual voice.
- Pair a distinctive display face with a readable body face.
- Use weight, scale, line-height, and tracking as design tools, not defaults.

### 2) Color and Theme
- Commit to a cohesive palette with clear hierarchy.
- Use CSS variables/tokens for repeatability.
- Favor strong dominant tones with intentional accents over timid, evenly distributed palettes.

### 3) Motion
- Animate with purpose: entry choreography, hover states, scroll reveals, state transitions.
- Prefer high-impact, orchestrated moments over noisy micro-animations.
- For React, use Motion when available; otherwise rely on robust CSS transitions/keyframes.
- Keep motion performant (`transform`, `opacity`) and respect reduced-motion preferences.

### 4) Spatial Composition
- Use deliberate composition choices: asymmetry, overlap, broken-grid placements, diagonal flows, controlled density, or large negative space.
- Layout must feel authored, not templated.

### 5) Background and Surface Detail
- Build atmosphere: gradients, mesh fields, noise/grain, transparency layering, decorative edges, shadow systems, pattern logic.
- Effects must match the concept rather than being decorative filler.

## Anti-Patterns (Never Ship)

- Cookie-cutter component arrangements with no point of view
- Overused "AI gradient hero on white" aesthetics
- Recycled font/palette pairings from common template culture
- Visual systems that ignore product context or user intent
- Elaborate visuals without functional clarity

## Complexity Matching

Match implementation depth to aesthetic ambition:

- **Maximalist / expressive direction**
  - Rich layering, deeper animation timelines, custom visuals, denser style logic
- **Minimal / refined direction**
  - Fewer elements, stronger rhythm, exact spacing, subtle but precise interactions

Do not underbuild expressive concepts or overbuild minimal concepts.

## Implementation Standards

- Deliver complete, runnable code for requested stack.
- Keep code maintainable: semantic structure, reusable classes/components, clear naming.
- Ensure responsive behavior across core breakpoints.
- Ensure keyboard/focus visibility and accessible semantics.
- Use design tokens (variables) for color, spacing, typography, radius, shadow, timing.
- Include states (default/hover/focus/active/disabled/loading where relevant).

## Response Structure

1. **Design direction** (2-5 bullets)

2. **Implementation**

3. **Polish notes**

- [ ] Motion is purposeful and performant

content.text:
The contour lines now come from the ground you are looking at, and the warp travels through the lines themselves.

Each card reads an 8 by 8 elevation grid, about 2 km across, from the same weather service already in the app. The strokes are the real isolines of that grid. A check near the middle of Toronto came back with 51 metres of relief, so those lines are the actual ground, not a drawn hill. The grid is kept for 6 hours. Ground with less than 4 metres of rise keeps a generated sheet, because real isolines there would collapse into a smudge.

The two cards share that survey and pick different intervals, so the drawings do not match. A slow sine wave then pushes each point along the line. The wave swells and eases, which is what turns a closed ring into an amoeba and lets it settle back toward the survey line. The title card moves farther and a little faster. The results card uses a smaller, slower current so the list stays easy to read. If the system asks for reduced motion, the lines stay on the survey.

content.text:
Health is up, and a study plan from Gemma is coming back again. `GET /api/health` returns the app up, with Gemma, voice, and Sentry all configured.

A fresh plan just took **5.9 seconds** and came back as a Gemma plan. Asking for that same place again took **2 milliseconds**, from the 30-minute memory cache. The earlier “Gemma did not answer” message was the sheet discarding a reply that never finished. Gemma 4 was spending the 500-token cap on an internal thought, so the plan itself was cut off. The deployed request now asks Google for minimal reasoning, so that cap is spent on the plan. If the reply arrives as a list, the plan object inside it is what gets read. A reply that still hits the cap is discarded, and the sheet keeps the notes it already showed.

The extra dev server on port **5173** is closed. Port **8787** is the app and the API. Live reload comes back with `npm run dev` when you want it. An older process on 8787 was stopped so this one could listen.

**Limits.** They matter, and the current caps are a reasonable fit for this app.

- Photon stays at three grouped lookups, 40 results each, the same budget for every reach, cached 30 minutes.
- Weather is cached 15 minutes. Elevation is cached 6 hours, and terrain is limited to 12 requests a minute.
- Gemma is one attempt, 20 seconds, no retry, then 30 minutes of memory for that place and medium.
- Readings are cached 30 minutes on the server and for the session in the browser.
- Per-minute caps are 40 searches, 30 place lookups, 10 nearby looks, 12 terrain grids, and 10 sign-ins. Plans are 12 per 10 minutes, readings 8 per 10 minutes.
- Sentry reports errors. In production it samples 10% of traces and profiles. Health checks are not sent. Coordinates stay out of the query string, and each trace is sent when the request finishes so the URL can be scrubbed first.

**Ollama.** Yes. The server reaches it only through `GEMMA_BASE_URL`. The example is `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`, and `GEMMA_MODEL` is any tag from `ollama list`. The Google id stays in the active example because that is the deployed app. The local block is commented, with `your-model-tag`. Your `.env` was left as you have it. For a local model, comment out the Google `GEMMA_MODEL` line and fill in the Ollama lines. A local server does not need the Google key.

**A ride and a drive.** They use the same result budget as the shorter reaches: up to 6 places in each group, 20 studies in total, one Photon look. On those two longer reaches the slots crowd toward the nearer places, and the farthest place in that set is still kept, so the longer distance remains visible. A 40 km look around the harbour returned 19 places: 17 of them within 8 km, and the farthest about 34 km. Here, a walk, and a hike stay evenly spaced through their shorter reach.

### Community Wisdom: [Why LLMs return invalid JSON — a language model has no parser](https://dev.to/sharpenlee/why-llms-return-invalid-json-a-language-model-has-no-parser-1n0d)
> **Source**: [sharpenlee](https://dev.to/sharpenlee)
> **Tags**: `json`, `ai`, `llm`, `programming`
>
> JSON mode promises syntax, and a reply cut off at `max_tokens` comes back with `finish_reason: length`. The post says to check that flag and discard the partial document. That matched this model: the cut-off replies were the ones the sheet was throwing away. The thread had no technical comments.
>
> 🔗 [Read Full Discussion](https://dev.to/sharpenlee/why-llms-return-invalid-json-a-language-model-has-no-parser-1n0d)

content.text:
A ride and a drive now spend the same result budget on the far places, and the Look button sits fully inside the title card.

**Farther reaches.** That choice holds. Here, a walk, and a hike are asks for what is close, so those stays are spaced from nearest to farthest. A ride and a drive are asks to look farther, so the same six places per kind go to the farthest ones found. A nearer place keeps a slot only when that kind has nothing farther out. The map frames the whole reach, so those places are on screen. A drive from the harbour just now listed places about 30 km out, and the map opened from the lake past Newmarket. The closer walk results were gone.

**Local models.** `GEMMA_BASE_URL` stays the setting. Empty means the deployed app, which calls Google’s Gemma. Ollama is still only `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`, and `GEMMA_MODEL` is whatever tag `ollama list` shows on that machine. The example says to comment out the Google id and put that tag in. If the base URL is local and the model name is empty, the server leaves it empty instead of guessing Gemma.

**Look.** The title card was clipping the button. The search field now gives up space, the button keeps its full width, and the desktop card has a floor so the row fits. Checked at a narrow desktop width and on a phone: the word Look is inside the card, with space between the button and the edge.

content.text:
The first place in the list now says why it is first, and a new visit starts by saying what Trail Sketch is for.

**Start here.** “Best today” was only “this row is first,” with no reason attached. The mark now names the reason:

- **For water** (or trees, buildings, sky, streets, hills) when that place matches what you picked to study.
- The feel word, such as **Quiet**, when you chose one in Refine.
- **Matches that** when a word you type fits the place.
- **Start here** when nothing else singled it out, so the nearest place in the reach leads.

Picking water put the dog fountain ahead of a plaza that is closer. The picks were already in the sort. The label never said so, which is why they felt idle.

**The word field.** It used to wait for a Match button, and a word like “trees” never met a park, because the park was not labeled with that word. Typing now reorders the list immediately. “Trees,” “water,” and “quiet” are real matches. The field stays inside Refine, so it is there when you want it and out of the way when you want the phone back in a pocket.

**Refine.** Opening it changes the button to **Show places**, and the same control sits at the top of the panel. On a phone the panel scrolls on its own and the place list keeps a share of the sheet.

**A first look.** Before any places, the screen reads: “Find a place, then put the phone away.” It says Trail Sketch looks for water, trees, stone, and open light, and that the things you pick lead the list. Back, on the place list, returns to that screen.

**The drag.** “Look around here” was sitting on the middle of the sheet’s top edge, which is why the sides still dragged and the center did not. The sheet now stops short of the title card, leaving a gap for that button, and the drag mark is a longer bar across the top of the list.

**Type.** Titles are Newsreader and the reading text is Source Serif 4. The small labels stay in IBM Plex Mono. The curled foot on letters such as J was the old display face.

content.text:
The plan is marked **AI**. That is the whole disclosure: the notes were generated, and the model name stays off the sheet. If it is busy or does not answer, the line is just as short: “AI is busy.” or “AI did not answer.”

The cards are warm paper with a canvas tooth. The graph-paper grid is gone. The little tab in the top-right corner of each card was a folded-page mark, not a control, so it is gone too.

### Community Wisdom: [AI Content Watermarking: Claude Starts Marking AI-Generated Content](https://dev.to/csfaas/ai-content-watermarking-claude-starts-marking-ai-generated-content-2407)
> **Source**: [csfaas](https://dev.to/csfaas)
> **Tags**: `ai`, `claude`, `llm`, `news`
>
> A visible “generated” mark is the familiar way to tell a reader the notes were produced by a model. Naming the model describes who processed the text, which is more than that mark needs to say. The thread had no comments.
>
> 🔗 [Read Full Discussion](https://dev.to/csfaas/ai-content-watermarking-claude-starts-marking-ai-generated-content-2407)

<available_subagent_types>
Available subagent_types and a quick description of what they do:
- generalPurpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. Use when searching for a keyword or file and not confident you'll find the match quickly.
- explore: Fast agent specialized for exploring codebases. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), search code for keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer questions about the codebase (eg. "how do API endpoints work?"). When calling this agent, specify the desired thoroughness level: "quick" for basic searches, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" for comprehensive analysis across multiple locations and naming conventions.
- cursor-guide: Read Cursor product documentation to answer questions about how Cursor Desktop, IDE, CLI, Cloud Agents, Bugbot, and other features work. Use when the user asks 'In Cursor, how do I...?' or similar questions about Cursor products.
- ci-investigator: Investigate a single failing PR CI check and return a short root-cause summary. Use when the user asks to summarize, explain, diagnose, or investigate a specific failed check from a pull request.
- bugbot: Use only when the user *explicitly* asks for a Bugbot-like review of local code changes. When launching this subagent, set the Task description to exactly "Bugbot". Launch exactly one Bugbot subagent with `run_in_background: false` unless the user explicitly asks to run in background. Use this fixed prompt form: "Full Repository Path: ...\nDiff: <one of: \"branch changes\", \"uncommitted changes\", \"natural language\">\nChange Description: ...\nCustom Instructions: ..."; default to `Diff: branch changes`; include `Change Description` only when `Diff` is `natural language`, formatting it as one block per changed file (a `<path> (added|modified|deleted|renamed)` header followed by bullets of what changed, mentioning line numbers or ranges inline where helpful), and only use `natural language` as a last resort after a regular diff-based review failed because the diff could not be computed; include `Custom Instructions` only when the user gave specific review instructions. This subagent is single-shot and does not support `resume`; always launch a fresh subagent instead.
- security-review: Use only when the user *explicitly* asks for a security review of local code changes. When launching this subagent, set the Task description to exactly "Security Review". Launch exactly one security-review subagent with `run_in_background: false` unless the user explicitly asks to run in background. Use this fixed prompt form: "Full Repository Path: ...\nDiff: <one of: \"branch changes\", \"uncommitted changes\">\nCustom Instructions: ..."; default to `Diff: branch changes`; include `Custom Instructions` only when the user gave specific review instructions. This subagent is single-shot and does not support `resume`; always launch a fresh subagent instead.
- best-of-n-runner: Run a task in an isolated git worktree. Each best-of-n-runner gets its own branch and working directory. Use for best-of-N parallel attempts or isolated experiments.
- ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications.
- deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline.
- performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance.
</available_subagent_types>

- inherit (default; required unless the user explicitly requested another model)

If the user isn't asking for a specific version, prefer the latest version of the model family. As an example, if the user just says "gpt" or "claude", use the latest available version of GPT or Claude.

IMPORTANT: If the user requests a model that is NOT in the list above, do NOT substitute a different model or guess. Instead, skip launching the subagent with that model and tell the user which model was unavailable and which models are available.

When speaking to the USER about which model you selected for a subagent, do NOT use the kebab-case model names unless the user requested the model using that format. Ue the same naming scheme the user used to discuss the model when they requested it.
</available_subagent_models>

<dynamic_tools>
You have access to tools through dynamic namespaces, e.g. MCP servers, using `GetDynamicTools` and `CallDynamicTool`.

## Dynamic Tool Discovery and Invocation

Use `GetDynamicTools` to discover tool schemas, then `CallDynamicTool` to invoke one tool. Aim to minimize round-trips: ideally one discovery call followed by one invocation.

If the user mentions a product or service represented by an available namespace, and the request likely depends on it, proactively inspect that namespace before answering. If you are unsure which namespace matches, search with a relevant pattern.

`GetDynamicTools` supports these modes:

1. `{"namespace":"<id>"}`: returns schemas and full descriptions for every tool in that namespace.
2. `{"namespace":"<id>","toolName":"<name>"}`: returns one tool schema with its full description.
3. `{"pattern":"<regex>"}`: searches namespace and tool names.
4. `{"namespace":"<id>","pattern":"<regex>"}`: searches tools within one namespace.
5. No arguments: returns the full catalog.

Pattern-search and catalog results shorten long descriptions, marked by a trailing "... [truncated]"; namespace and single-tool lookups always return the complete description.

Always inspect a tool's schema before invoking it with `CallDynamicTool`.

If the available dynamic tools do not fully support what the user asked you to do, complete the work you can with the current tool set. In your work summary, include what you were unable to do and why. Do not use browser automation to work around missing tools unless the user explicitly asks you to use the browser.

Available dynamic tool namespaces:

<namespace name="cursor-ide-browser" tools="browser_navigate, browser_snapshot, browser_click, browser_mouse_click_xy, browser_type, browser_fill, browser_select_option, browser_press_key, browser_scroll, browser_drag, browser_get_bounding_box, browser_highlight, browser_tabs, browser_cdp, browser_take_screenshot, browser_lock" namespaceUseInstructions="The cursor-ide-browser MCP server provides a Cursor-owned browser tab plus a raw Chrome DevTools Protocol command tool.

CORE WORKFLOW:
1. Start by understanding the user's goal and what success looks like on the page.
2. Use browser_tabs with action "list" to inspect open tabs and URLs before acting.
3. Use browser_navigate to create or navigate the target tab. Omit the position parameter for background automation so focus is preserved.
4. Use browser_lock before longer automation on an existing tab, then browser_lock with action "unlock" when finished.
5. Use browser_snapshot for accessibility context and browser_take_screenshot for visual verification.
6. Use browser_click, browser_type, browser_fill, browser_select_option, browser_press_key, browser_scroll, and browser_drag for page interactions.
7. Use browser_highlight and browser_get_bounding_box for visual grounding and coordinate diagnostics.
8. Use browser_cdp for page inspection, profiling, runtime evaluation, DOM/CSS queries, and performance data.

AVOID RABBIT HOLES:
1. Do not repeat the same failing action more than once without new evidence such as a fresh snapshot, a different ref, a changed page state, or a clear new hypothesis.
2. IMPORTANT: If four attempts fail or progress stalls, stop acting and report what you observed, what blocked progress, and the most likely next step.
3. Prefer gathering evidence over brute force. If the page is confusing, use browser_snapshot, browser_take_screenshot, or CDP inspection before trying more actions.
4. If you encounter a blocker such as login, passkey/manual user interaction, permissions, captchas, destructive confirmations, missing data, or an unexpected state, stop and report it instead of improvising repeated actions.
5. Do not get stuck in wait-action-wait loops. Every retry should be justified by something newly observed.

CRITICAL - Lock/unlock workflow:
1. browser_lock requires an existing browser tab - you CANNOT call browser_lock with action: "lock" before browser_navigate
2. Correct order: browser_navigate -> browser_lock({ action: "lock" }) -> (interactions) -> browser_lock({ action: "unlock" })
3. If a browser tab already exists (check with browser_tabs list), call browser_lock with action: "lock" FIRST before any interactions
4. Only call browser_lock with action: "unlock" when completely done with ALL browser operations for this turn

IMPORTANT - Waiting strategy:
When waiting for page changes, prefer short CDP polling loops with Runtime.evaluate, DOM queries, Page lifecycle signals, or browser_snapshot checks rather than a single long wait.

CDP USAGE:
- Use browser_cdp with a DevTools Protocol method and params object, for example Runtime.evaluate, DOM.getDocument, CSS.getComputedStyleForNode, Profiler.start/stop, Performance.getMetrics, Log.enable, and Network.enable.
- Do not use browser_cdp with CDP Input.* methods. They are denied because they are focus-sensitive in Electron webviews and can route input to Cursor UI instead of the browser page.
- Use browser_click, browser_type, browser_fill, browser_select_option, browser_press_key, browser_scroll, and browser_drag for clicks, typing, filling inputs, selecting options, keyboard actions, scrolling, and drag-and-drop.
- Use Runtime.evaluate for advanced DOM-scoped interactions that the dedicated browser tools do not cover.
- For profiling, call Profiler.enable, Profiler.start, reproduce the behavior, then Profiler.stop. The profile is saved to a file and returned as a log_file; read that file only when you need to inspect details.
- For JavaScript evaluation, prefer Runtime.evaluate with returnByValue when possible.
- Device emulation you set with Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride, Emulation.setTouchEmulationEnabled, or Emulation.setUserAgentOverride (for example for a phone-sized screenshot) lasts only for the current turn: it is cleared when your turn ends, and the user can reset it from the browser tab at any time. Send Emulation.clearDeviceMetricsOverride yourself once you are done with it within a turn.
- Some browser-wide or sensitive CDP methods are denied, especially cookie, storage, permission, download, target-management, filesystem-backed file-input commands, system-level commands, and CDP navigation/history navigation commands.
- Large CDP responses are saved to files instead of being inlined. Prefer using the returned file path over immediately stuffing large payloads into context; read focused sections only when needed.

VISION:
- browser_take_screenshot attaches an image result that the model can inspect. CDP Page.captureScreenshot returns data inside JSON and should not replace browser_take_screenshot when visual verification is needed.

NOTES:
- browser_snapshot returns snapshot YAML and is the main source of truth for page structure.
- Refs are opaque handles tied to the latest browser_snapshot for that tab.
- Iframe content is not accessible - only elements outside iframes can be interacted with.

content.text:
The grain is gone, and a written plan now says what it is.

The map is the watercolor field map again. The noise and the graph paper were sitting under every wash, which made the streets look speckled. Land is painted a warm paper color, so the city reads as a map. The cards are the same warm paper, plain, with the hard offset shadow.

On a study, the line above the tones says **AI wrote this plan.** It names the work: these notes were written for this place. While that is happening the card says "Writing a plan for this place." If it fails, the message is about the plan ("The plan did not come back."), and the model stays unnamed. The first-visit guide uses the same voice as the rest of the app: how far, a place, then a plan.

Motion is tied to those moments. Opening a place still lifts the sheet, a dropped pin still lands, and buttons still press. When a written plan is on the card, that line and the tones settle in once. People who prefer reduced motion get the content without the movement.

I checked this on the desktop layout and at a phone width. The saved study for Butterfield Park showed "AI wrote this plan." above its tones, and the streets around it were an even wash. The app is serving on port 8787.

## Community Wisdom

Ken Imoto, in [Framer Motion + View Transitions API: 4 UI Motion Patterns That Stop Looking AI-Generated](https://dev.to/kenimo49/framer-motion-view-transitions-api-4-ui-motion-patterns-that-stop-looking-ai-generated-25gg), argues that the default fade-on-everything has motion and no intent, and that a curve should mean something. The plan note and the tones use that idea: one arrival, on the curve the rest of the app already uses (`--ease-curve`). The place list stays still, because that stagger is for a page you read from top to bottom, and this list is something you scan. Phong Designs AI System [replied](https://dev.to/kenimo49/framer-motion-view-transitions-api-4-ui-motion-patterns-that-stop-looking-ai-generated-25gg) that loose timing numbers get "cleaned up" later, and that reduced motion is the only check that can actually fail. The new arrival uses the named curve, and the reduced-motion rule turns it off.
Briefly inform the user about the task result and perform any follow-up actions (if needed). If there's no follow-ups needed, don't explicitly say that.
The first rebuild finished successfully. The app already picked up that build, plus a later one, and is serving the quieter map and the “AI wrote this plan.” note on port 8787.
